section.title: 6. Offline Safe RL: CPQ, COptiDICE, CDT, FISOR

items.source_snippet:
Key equation — The COptiDICE objective (Lee et al. 2022, Eqs. 4–12)
Regularise the constrained LP with an $f$-divergence (see Primer C) to the data distribution ($f$ strictly convex, $f(1)=0$, $d^{\mathcal D}\gt0$): $$ egin{aligned}\max_{d\ge0}\ \ &\mathbb E_{d}[R]-\alpha\,D_f(d\,\|\,d^{\mathcal D})\ ext{s.t.}\ \ &\mathbb E_d[C_k]\le\hat c_k,\ &\sum_{a'}d(s',a')=(1-\gamma)p_0(s')+\gamma\sum_{s,a}d(s,a)T(s'\mid s,a)\ \ orall s',\end{aligned}$$ with $D_f(d\|d^{\mathcal D})=\mathbb E_{d^{\mathcal D}}[f(d/d^{\mathcal D})]$. With $w=d/d^{\mathcal D}$ and $e_{\lambda, u}(s,a)=R(s,a)-\lambda^{ op}C(s,a)+\gamma\,\mathbb E_{s'\sim T(s,a)}[ u(s')]- u(s)$, $$ egin{aligned}\min_{\lambda\ge0,\ u}\ \max_{w\ge0}\ &\mathbb E_{(s,a)\sim d^{\mathcal D}} ig[w(s,a)\,e_{\lambda, u}(s,a)-\alpha f(w(s,a)) ig]\ &+(1-\gamma)\,\mathbb E_{s_0\sim p_0}[ u(s_0)]+\lambda^{ op}\hat c,\end{aligned}$$ $$w^\ast_{\lambda, u}(s,a)=\Big((f')^{-1} ig( frac1\alpha e_{\lambda, u}(s,a) ig)\Big)_+ ,$$ for $\alpha\gt0$ (Step 3 of the derivation below says when this clipped formula is valid), and substituting $w^\ast$ leaves a convex minimisation over $(\lambda, u)$ alone. Every term is an expectation over the dataset, so the problem is fully offline; the one catch is the conditional expectation over $s'$ inside $e_{\lambda, u}$, which the practical single-sample loss only upper-bounds unless transitions are deterministic (see the derivation).

items.label: Theorem — KL-robust cost estimation with Bellman-flow compatibility (Lee et al. 2022, Prop. 2, finite-support version)

section.title: 6. Offline Safe RL: CPQ, COptiDICE, CDT, FISOR

items.source_snippet:
Theorem — KL-robust cost estimation with Bellman-flow compatibility (Lee et al. 2022, Prop. 2, finite-support version)

Fix finite tuple support $x=(s_0,s,a,s')$, a positive reference law $q(x)$, a fixed nonnegative ratio $w(s,a)$, bounded cost $C$, and $0\le\gamma\lt1$. Put $b_y(x)=(1-\gamma)\mathbf1[s_0=y]+w(s,a)(\gamma\mathbf1[s'=y]-\mathbf1[s=y])$. For $\epsilon\gt0$ define $\mathcal U=\{p\ge0:\sum_xp(x)=1,\ D_{\rm KL}(p\|q)\le\epsilon,\ \mathbb E_p b_y=0\ \forall y\}$. If this set has a relative-interior point with KL strictly below $\epsilon$, then

$$\sup_{p\in\mathcal U}\mathbb E_p[wC]=\inf_{\tau\ge0,\chi}\left\{\tau\epsilon+\tau\log\mathbb E_q\exp\!\left(\frac{wC+\sum_y\chi(y)b_y}{\tau}\right)\right\}.$$

At $\tau=0$ use the limit of the log-sum-exp term, not division by zero. The $b_y$ equations enforce discounted flow for the weighted occupancy. The true normalised policy cost is bounded by this supremum only on an event where a law $p_{\rm true}\in\mathcal U$ also makes $wp_{\rm true}(s,a)$ that policy’s true occupancy. Finite support and strict feasibility justify duality; inclusion supplies the statistical interpretation. A fitted ratio or a chosen radius alone supplies neither inclusion nor coverage.

The adversary reallocates data mass towards expensive compatible transitions. Its dual replaces a search over distributions by a temperature and a state potential.

Lee et al. 2022.

items.label: Theorem — Feasibility-guided optimal policy (FISOR, Defs. 1–4 and Thm. 1)

section.title: 6. Offline Safe RL: CPQ, COptiDICE, CDT, FISOR

items.source_snippet:
Theorem — Feasibility-guided optimal policy (FISOR, Defs. 1–4 and Thm. 1)
Feasible values. $V_h^\ast(s)=\min_\pi\max_{t\in\mathbb N}h(s_t)$ with $s_0=s$ (the worst future violation under the best policy) and $Q_h^\ast$ likewise; the largest feasible region is $S_f^\ast=\{s:V_h^\ast(s)\le0\}$. It is learned offline from the discounted feasible Bellman operator $(\mathcal P^\ast Q)(s,a)=(1-\gamma)h(s)+\gamma\max\big\{h(s),\min_{a'}Q(s',a')\big\}$, with $s'$ the successor of $(s,a)$. This is a contraction in the sup norm on bounded functions (theorem below, with the separate limit $\gamma\uparrow1$). The paper writes the inner minimum as $V_h^\ast(s')$; there it means $\min_{a'}Q(s',a')$ of the current iterate, not the true $V_h^\ast$ defined above. The minimum over next actions is approximated in-sample by reversed expectile regression, so that no out-of-distribution action is queried.
Decoupled problem. Fix a state $s$, let $p_0=\pi_\beta(\cdot\mid s)$, $A_r^\ast=Q_r^\ast-V_r^\ast$, $A_h^\ast=Q_h^\ast-V_h^\ast$ (bounded tables), and let $\alpha_1,\alpha_2\gt0$ be inverse temperatures (larger values concentrate probability more strongly). In a feasible state ($V_h^\ast(s)\le0$) maximise $\sum_ap(a)A_r^\ast(s,a)-\alpha_1^{-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|p_0)$ over distributions $p$ on the safe actions $S_s=\{a:Q_h^\ast(s,a)\le0\}$, assuming $p_0(S_s)\gt0$; in an infeasible state minimise $\sum_ap(a)A_h^\ast(s,a)+\alpha_2^{-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|p_0)$.
Statement (Thm. 1). The optimal solution is weighted behaviour cloning, $\pi^\ast(a\mid s)\propto\pi_\beta(a\mid s)\,w(s,a)$, with $$w(s,a)=\begin{cases}\exp\big(\alpha_1A_r^\ast(s,a)\big)\,\mathbf 1\big[Q_h^\ast(s,a)\le0\big], & V_h^\ast(s)\le0,\\ \exp\big(-\alpha_2A_h^\ast(s,a)\big), & V_h^\ast(s)\gt0,\end{cases}$$ normalised by $Z(s)=\sum_a\pi_\beta(a\mid s)w(s,a)$, which is positive exactly when the behaviour policy gives mass to a safe action (weighted cloning cannot create safe actions the data never took). Proof: substituting $p^\ast$ turns the gap to any other admissible $p$ into $\alpha_i^{-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|p^\ast)\ge0$, the Gibbs argument of FOCOPS. Exact safety additionally needs the exact undiscounted feasibility values; approximate critics and a finite diffusion fit do not inherit the hard mask automatically.
In words. Inside the region from which the constraint can be kept forever, imitate the rewarding actions that keep you inside; outside it, imitate the actions that reduce the violation fastest. The same Gibbs reweighting as FOCOPS, with a hard feasibility mask instead of a price.

items.label: Theorem — The discounted feasibility operator: contraction and the limit $\gamma\uparrow1$ (finite deterministic case)

section.title: 6. Offline Safe RL: CPQ, COptiDICE, CDT, FISOR

items.source_snippet:
Theorem — The discounted feasibility operator: contraction and the limit $\gamma\uparrow1$ (finite deterministic case)

Assume a deterministic finite-state, finite-action system $s'=f(s,a)$, a nonempty action set at each state, bounded $h$, and $0\lt\gamma\lt1$. On real-valued state-action tables write FISOR's operator $\mathcal P^\ast$ as $T_\gamma Q=(1-\gamma)h(s)+\gamma\max\{h(s),\min_{a'}Q(f(s,a),a')\}$. Then $\|T_\gamma Q-T_\gamma\widetilde Q\|_\infty\le\gamma\|Q-\widetilde Q\|_\infty$. There is a unique fixed point $Q_\gamma$, and $\|T_\gamma^kQ_0-Q_\gamma\|_\infty\le\gamma^k\|Q_0-Q_\gamma\|_\infty$. In this finite deterministic setting, $Q_\gamma\to Q_h^*$ as $\gamma\uparrow1$, with $Q_h^*(s,a)=\inf_\pi\sup_{t\ge0}h(s_t)$ after initial action $a$.

Proof sketch. $|\max\{h,x\}-\max\{h,y\}|\le|x-y|$ and $|\min_{a'}Q(s',a')-\min_{a'}\widetilde Q(s',a')|\le\max_{a'}|Q(s',a')-\widetilde Q(s',a')|$, so min and max cannot enlarge the largest input error, and the factor $\gamma$ shrinks it (Banach fixed point, Primer 0). For the separate discount limit, a fixed stationary policy eventually repeats a state; the maximum on its finite prefix and cycle is attained in finite time. Its discounted stopping value tends to this maximum. There are finitely many deterministic stationary policies, so the limit commutes with their minimum. This also ensures the viability infimum is attained. Continuous or stochastic systems need additional assumptions and a specified safety semantics. A negative finite-discount estimate alone is not an undiscounted sign certificate.

For example, a forced transition from $h(s_0)=-1$ to an absorbing state with $h(s_1)=0.1$ gives $Q_{1/2}(s_1)=0.1$ and $Q_{1/2}(s_0)=-0.5+0.5(0.1)=-0.45$, but the undiscounted maximum is $0.1\gt0$.

The operator is FISOR's (Zheng et al., ICLR 2024); the limit statement and its proof sketch are the elementary finite deterministic case.

For the separate discount limit, a fixed stationary policy eventually repeats a state; the maximum on its finite prefix and cycle is attained in finite time. Its discounted stopping value tends to this maximum. There are finitely many deterministic stationary policies, so the limit commutes with their minimum. This also ensures the viability infimum is attained. Continuous or stochastic systems need additional assumptions and a specified safety semantics. A negative finite-discount estimate alone is not an undiscounted sign certificate.For example, a forced transition from $h(s_0)=-1$ to an absorbing state with $h(s_1)=0.1$ gives $Q_{1/2}(s_1)=0.1$ and $Q_{1/2}(s_0)=-0.5+0.5(0.1)=-0.45$, but the undiscounted maximum is $0.1\gt0$.The operator is FISOR's (Zheng et al., ICLR 2024); the limit statement and its proof sketch are the elementary finite deterministic case.

items.source_snippet:
Theorem — A sufficient cost-transfer bound for training on shaped data (derived here; the argument behind OASIS, Thms. 1–2)

This is a self-contained sufficient version of the distribution-transfer argument used by OASIS, not the paper's own statement. Assume $0\le c\le C_{\max}$, $0\lt\gamma\lt1$, and a feasible comparator $\pi^*$ with $J_c(\pi^*)\le\kappa$. Let the generated joint law be $d_g(s)\pi_g(a\mid s)$ and assume $d_g$ is the true normalised occupancy of $\pi_g$ in the same MDP. Suppose

$$D_{\rm TV}(d_g,d^{\pi^*})\le e_s,\quad\mathbb E_{d^{\pi^*}}D_{\rm KL}(\pi_g\|\pi^*)\le e_i,\quad\mathbb E_{d_g}D_{\rm KL}(\pi_\phi\|\pi_g)\le e_r.$$

Then the joint shaping error is at most $e_s+\sqrt{e_i/2}$ and

$$J_c(\pi_\phi)-\kappa\le\frac{2C_{\max}}{1-\gamma}(e_s+\sqrt{e_i/2})+\frac{2C_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^2}\sqrt{e_r/2}.$$

Proof. For joint laws, $D_{\mathrm{TV}}(d_g\pi_g,d^{\pi^\ast}\pi^\ast)\le D_{\mathrm{TV}}(d_g,d^{\pi^\ast})+\mathbb E_{d^{\pi^\ast}}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_g\|\pi^\ast)$, and Pinsker plus Jensen bound the last term by $\sqrt{e_i/2}$. Since $J_c(\pi)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{d^\pi\pi}[c]$ and $|\mathbb E_pc-\mathbb E_qc|\le2C_{\max}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)$, this gives $J_c(\pi_g)-J_c(\pi^\ast)\le\frac{2C_{\max}}{1-\gamma}(e_s+\sqrt{e_i/2})$. For $\pi_\phi$ versus $\pi_g$, the joint laws differ by at most $\|d^{\pi_\phi}-d_g\|_1+2\mathbb E_{d_g}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_\phi\|\pi_g)\le\frac{2}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{d_g}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_\phi\|\pi_g)$ in $\ell_1$ (Step 4 of Section 2), and Pinsker plus Jensen give the $\sqrt{e_r/2}$ term; finally $J_c(\pi^\ast)\le\kappa$. This explains why realistic generated transitions and small fit error both matter.

The source’s diffusion theorem seeks $e_s=\widetilde O(\varepsilon_{\rm score}\sqrt K)+C(d^*,L,K)$, assuming an $L$-Lipschitz score $\nabla\log d^*$, finite second moment, an appropriate target condition, controlled score error and inverse-policy KL error. Here $K$ is diffusion time, not policy updates; the unspecified remainder prevents a numerical certificate. Its printed cost proof additionally replaces the learned policy occupancy by the dataset marginal and moves a KL average between different state weightings. Those steps need coverage/compatibility assumptions. The explicit bound above states a sufficient occupancy condition and retains a distribution-shift factor instead of silently making those replacements. Synthetic data do not automatically satisfy that condition.

Compare Yao et al., NeurIPS 2024, Thms. 1–2.

items.label: Theorem — Exact SB-TRPO lexicographic value convergence (Wagner, Kanwar & Ong 2025, Thm. 1)

section.title: 7. Benchmarks, Reproducibility and the 2026 State of the Art

items.source_snippet:
Theorem — Exact SB-TRPO lexicographic value convergence (Wagner, Kanwar & Ong 2025, Thm. 1)

Assume a finite discounted MDP, bounded rewards and nonnegative costs, a fixed initial distribution, $0\lt\gamma\lt1$, the full class of stationary stochastic policies, a fixed radius $\delta\gt0$ and fixed $\beta\in(0,1]$. Start with any policy. Use the old-first divergence $K_k(\pi)=\mathbb E_{s\sim d^{\pi_k}}D_{\rm KL}(\pi_k\|\pi)[s]$, exact values, and globally attained optimisers:

$$c_k^*=\min_{K_k(\pi)\le\delta}J_c(\pi),\qquad \pi_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{\substack{K_k(\pi)\le\delta\\J_c(\pi)\le(1-\beta)J_c(\pi_k)+\beta c_k^*}}J_r(\pi).$$

Then $J_c(\pi_k)\to J_c^*:=\min_\pi J_c(\pi)$. If $\beta\lt1$, also $J_r(\pi_k)\to\max_{J_c(\pi)=J_c^*}J_r(\pi)$. These are convergence statements for values, not necessarily for policy parameters. Zero cost is the limit only when a zero-cost policy exists.

Each step must take a fixed fraction of the cost improvement available locally, preventing it from settling at a cost-suboptimal policy. When $\beta\lt1$, the remaining freedom permits reward improvement among cost-minimal policies. Exact optimisation over the full policy class and a fixed positive radius are the essential idealisations; a neural surrogate step is outside this theorem.

Wagner, Kanwar & Ong 2025.

items.label: Caveat — No method dominates, and benchmark safety is not a guarantee

section.title: 7. Benchmarks, Reproducibility and the 2026 State of the Art

items.source_snippet:
Caveat — No method dominates, and benchmark safety is not a guarantee
Read across the papers above (each under its own protocol; no single controlled comparison exists), model-based agents report the strongest results on vision-only tasks, redesigned trust-region methods on last-iterate safety, and feasibility-based methods on state-wise and strict offline limits (at a price in return); each ranking moves with the cost limit, the metric and the seed count. Every "safe" number above is an average (over episodes, seeds and often over training) of an expected or counted cost on a simulator: it says nothing about individual trajectories, rare catastrophic events, or the physical system the policy will eventually control (the guarantee types of Module 1). The statements in this module that deserve the word guarantee come in two kinds: safety-during-learning theorems (ActSafe's Theorem 4.8; SOOPER's claims remain subject to the switching-time gap in Section 5), which hold on a calibration event that rests on an RKHS-norm bound you must trust; and optimisation results (the per-step worst-case bounds of CPO, PCPO and C-TRPO, CRPO's tabular convergence rates), which hold for idealised exact or tabular updates, not for the deep-RL algorithm that runs. Hard state constraints at every step are the business of safety filters and reachability (see Module 10).

items.label: Exercise 9.P1 — Easy: Center an advantage under the old policy
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P1 — Easy: Center an advantage under the old policy

At one state let $Q^\pi=(5,1)$ and $\pi=(1/4,3/4)$. Compute $V^\pi$ and the two advantages. What is their expectation under $\pi$? Under $\pi'=(1/2,1/2)$, what is the average advantage?

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
The state value is the old-policy average of the action values.
Show answer

$V^\pi=(1/4)5+(3/4)1=2$. Subtracting gives advantages $(3,-1)$. Their old-policy average is $(1/4)3+(3/4)(-1)=0$, as the advantage definition requires. The new-policy average is $(1/2)3+(1/2)(-1)=1$. The new policy shifts probability toward the action better than the old average; converting this local quantity to return also involves discounted visitation.

items.label: Exercise 9.P2 — Easy: Measure a change in action probabilities
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P2 — Easy: Measure a change in action probabilities

For old probabilities $(1/2,1/2)$ and new probabilities $(3/4,1/4)$, compute total variation and the KL divergence of new relative to old, using natural logs.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
Total variation is half the sum of absolute differences. KL weights each log ratio by its new probability.
Show answer

Total variation is $\tfrac12(|3/4-1/2|+|1/4-1/2|)=1/4$. The KL divergence is

$$\tfrac34\log(3/2)+\tfrac14\log(1/2)\approx0.130812.$$

Both vanish for identical distributions, but they measure change differently. KL is not symmetric; the direction specified in the question matters.

items.label: Exercise 9.P3 — Easy: Read the axes of a trust-region ellipse
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P3 — Easy: Read the axes of a trust-region ellipse

Let $H=\mathrm{diag}(4,1)$ and $\delta=1/2$. Rewrite $\tfrac12x^\top Hx\le\delta$ in coordinates, find the axis radii, and check $x=(1/2,0)$.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
Expand the diagonal quadratic form and cancel the common factor $1/2$.
Show answer

The inequality becomes $4x_1^2+x_2^2\le1$. Setting $x_2=0$ gives $|x_1|\le1/2$; setting $x_1=0$ gives $|x_2|\le1$. The axes have radii $1/2$ and $1$. At $(1/2,0)$, the quadratic form is $1$, hence the original left side is $1/2=\delta$: this point is on the boundary. Larger curvature in the first direction permits a smaller step.

items.label: Exercise 9.P4 — Easy: Check a linearized cost constraint
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P4 — Easy: Check a linearized cost constraint

The current cost residual is $c=-0.2$ and its gradient is $b=(1,0)$. Test $c+b^\top x\le0$ at $x=(0.3,0.1)$ and $x=(0.1,0.1)$. What does this check actually certify?

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
The second coordinate does not contribute because its gradient coefficient is zero.
Show answer

The first predicted residual is $-0.2+0.3=0.1$, which violates the linearized constraint. The second is $-0.2+0.1=-0.1$, which passes. This certifies feasibility of a local affine approximation, not of the true nonlinear cost. Curvature and estimation error need separate bounds or an actual acceptance check.

items.label: Exercise 9.P5 — Medium: Solve the unconstrained trust-region step
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P5 — Medium: Solve the unconstrained trust-region step

Maximize $g^\top x$ subject to $\tfrac12x^\top Hx\le1/2$, with $g=(1,2)$ and $H=\mathrm{diag}(1,4)$. Use $x=\sqrt{2\delta/(g^\top H^{-1}g)}\,H^{-1}g$ and verify the solution.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
First compute $H^{-1}g$ and its dot product with $g$.
Show answer

$H^{-1}=\mathrm{diag}(1,1/4)$, so $H^{-1}g=(1,1/2)$ and $g^\top H^{-1}g=2$. Thus $x=(1/\sqrt2,1/(2\sqrt2))$. Its quadratic form is $1/2+4(1/8)=1$, meeting the constraint boundary. The objective is $1/\sqrt2+1/\sqrt2=\sqrt2$. Cauchy–Schwarz in the $H$ metric bounds every feasible objective by $\sqrt{(g^\top H^{-1}g)(x^\top Hx)}\le\sqrt2$, proving optimality.

Exercise 9.P6 — Medium: Project a proposed step onto a cost half-space

Find the Euclidean projection of $y=(0.6,0.2)$ onto $\{x:x_1\le0.1\}$. Compute the displacement and the objective $\tfrac12\|x-y\|^2$.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
The second coordinate is unrestricted, so changing it only increases the distance.
Show answer

The nearest feasible first coordinate is the boundary $x_1=0.1$, and $x_2$ remains $0.2$. Thus $x=(0.1,0.2)$ and $x-y=(-0.5,0)$. The distance is $0.5$ and the objective is $\tfrac12(0.5)^2=0.125$. A projection repairs the constraint with the smallest change in the chosen metric; another metric can produce another correction.

items.label: Exercise 9.P7 — Medium: See how discounting enlarges a bound
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P7 — Medium: See how discounting enlarges a bound

A surrogate error is bounded by $2\gamma\varepsilon v/(1-\gamma)^2$, with valid advantage bound $\varepsilon=0.5$ and average total variation $v=0.01$. Evaluate this expression at $\gamma=0.9$ and $\gamma=0.5$.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
Evaluate the squared denominator before dividing. Here $\varepsilon$ and $v$ are held fixed.
Show answer

At $0.9$, the numerator is $2(0.9)(0.5)(0.01)=0.009$ and denominator is $0.1^2=0.01$, giving $0.9$. At $0.5$, they are $0.005$ and $0.5^2=0.25$, giving $0.02$. The first bound is $45$ times larger. A small policy change can therefore have a loose worst-case return bound at a long effective horizon; this calculation describes the bound, not the actual error.

items.label: Exercise 9.P8 — Medium: Apply a pessimistic model cost check
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P8 — Medium: Apply a pessimistic model cost check

On a stated confidence event, true policy cost satisfies $J_c\le\widehat J_c+2$. The budget is $8$. Can estimates $7$ and $5$ certify feasibility on that event? Does failure of the check prove a policy is unsafe?

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
Compare the upper bound, rather than the estimate, with the budget.
Show answer

An estimate of $7$ gives upper bound $9\gt8$, so the stated bound cannot certify that policy. An estimate of $5$ gives upper bound $7\le8$, so that policy is feasible on the confidence event. The failed first check does not prove true cost exceeds $8$: it may be below the upper bound. The probability of the resulting certificate is inherited from the confidence event, which must cover this policy evaluation.

items.label: Exercise 9.P9 — Hard: Solve a cost-constrained step on a disk
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P9 — Hard: Solve a cost-constrained step on a disk

Maximize $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1^2+x_2^2\le1$ and $x_1\le0.2$. Find the optimizer and explain why simply taking the unconstrained trust-region direction fails.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
For a fixed $x_1=t$, the best allowed $x_2$ is $\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Maximize the resulting one-variable function over $-1\le t\le0.2$.
Show answer

Without the cost constraint, the optimum is $(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$, whose first coordinate exceeds $0.2$. On the upper disk boundary, the objective is $f(t)=t+\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Its derivative is $1-t/\sqrt{1-t^2}$, positive for $-1\lt t\le0.2$. Therefore its maximum on the allowed interval occurs at $t=0.2$.

The optimizer is $(0.2,\sqrt{0.96})\approx(0.2,0.979796)$, with objective approximately $1.179796$. Both the disk and cost constraints are active; the gradient direction alone does not account for their intersection.

items.label: Exercise 9.P10 — Hard: Audit a linearized boundary step
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P10 — Hard: Audit a linearized boundary step

The true cost residual is $J_c(x)-d=-0.1+x+2x^2$. Linearize at $x=0$. A step $x=0.1$ reaches the linearized boundary. Is it truly feasible? Find the largest nonnegative feasible step.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
Retain the quadratic remainder for the true check, and solve $2x^2+x-0.1=0$.
Show answer

The linearization is $-0.1+x$, which is zero at $0.1$. But the true residual there is $-0.1+0.1+2(0.1)^2=0.02\gt0$, so the step is infeasible. The positive root is

$$x_{\max}=\frac{-1+\sqrt{1.8}}4\approx0.085410.$$

The quadratic increases for $x\ge0$, so feasible nonnegative steps are exactly $0\le x\le x_{\max}$. The discarded curvature term explains the violation. A local subproblem needs an error margin or line search to transfer its prediction to the true constraint.

items.label: Exercise 9.P11 — Hard: Check support before importance weighting
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P11 — Hard: Check support before importance weighting

The data policy chooses two actions with probabilities $(0.99,0.01)$; the candidate uses $(0.5,0.5)$. Find both likelihood ratios and their expectation under the data policy. What changes if its second probability is zero?

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
The ratio is candidate probability divided by data probability for the same action.
Show answer

The ratios are $0.5/0.99=50/99$ and $0.5/0.01=50$. Their old-policy average is $0.99(50/99)+0.01(50)=0.5+0.5=1$. The rare action receives a large weight, making estimates sensitive to few observations even though the normalization is correct.

If the data policy assigns zero probability to the second action while the candidate assigns $0.5$, the ratio is undefined there and data provide no samples of that action. The usual importance-sampling identity requires candidate support to be contained in data-policy support; an extrapolated critic does not repair that missing statistical assumption.

items.label: Exercise 9.P12 — Hard: Combine reward and cost confidence statements
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.P12 — Hard: Combine reward and cost confidence statements

A proposed update has predicted return improvement $0.4$ with error at most $0.3$ on event $E_r$ of probability at least $0.98$. Its cost estimate is $7$ with upward error at most $0.5$ on event $E_c$ of probability at least $0.97$. Budget is $8$. Give a joint guarantee without assuming independence.

Review this topic · Revisit the prerequisite

Show hint
Use the union bound on failure events, then apply both numerical margins on their intersection.
Show answer

The union bound gives $\mathbb P(E_r\cap E_c)\ge1-0.02-0.03=0.95$. On that joint event, true improvement is at least $0.4-0.3=0.1\gt0$, and true cost is at most $7+0.5=7.5\le8$. Hence the update improves reward and satisfies the budget with probability at least $0.95$, provided the two events apply to this selected update. No independence was used; multiplying the two success probabilities would require it.

items.label: Exercise 9.1 — The performance difference lemma, algebraically
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.1 — The performance difference lemma, algebraically

Finite MDP, stationary policies $\pi,\pi'$. Write $P_{\pi'}(s,s')=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a)$ (row-stochastic, acting on value vectors; Section 2 used its transpose), $r_{\pi'}(s)=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)r(s,a)$ and $\bar a(s)=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)A^\pi(s,a)$. (a) Show that $\bar a=r_{\pi'}+\gamma P_{\pi'}V^\pi-V^\pi$. (b) Deduce $V^{\pi'}-V^\pi=(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a$, and from it the performance difference lemma with its factor $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$. (c) Two states $\{0,1\}$, deterministic actions stay and switch, reward 1 per step in state 1, $\gamma=\tfrac12$, start in state 0. $\pi$ switches with probability $\tfrac12$ in both states; $\pi'$ switches in state 0 and stays in state 1. Compute $A^\pi$, $\bar a$, $d^{\pi'}$ and $d^\pi$, check the lemma, and explain why the surrogate $L_\pi(\pi')$ happens to be exact here.

Show answer
(a) $\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)Q^\pi(s,a)=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)\big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V^\pi(s')\big]=r_{\pi'}(s)+\gamma(P_{\pi'}V^\pi)(s)$; subtract $V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)V^\pi(s)$.
(b) The Bellman equation of $\pi'$ is $V^{\pi'}=r_{\pi'}+\gamma P_{\pi'}V^{\pi'}$. Subtract $V^\pi$ and add and subtract $\gamma P_{\pi'}V^\pi$: $V^{\pi'}-V^\pi=\underbrace{r_{\pi'}+\gamma P_{\pi'}V^\pi-V^\pi}_{=\bar a}+\gamma P_{\pi'}(V^{\pi'}-V^\pi)$. Since $\|\gamma P_{\pi'}\|_\infty=\gamma\lt1$, $I-\gamma P_{\pi'}$ is invertible with Neumann series $\sum_t\gamma^tP_{\pi'}^t$, so $V^{\pi'}-V^\pi=(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a$. Multiply by $\mu^{\top}$: $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\mu^{\top}(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a=\sum_t\gamma^t(\mu^{\top}P_{\pi'}^t)\bar a$, and $\mu^{\top}P_{\pi'}^t$ is the law of $s_t$ under $\pi'$, so $(1-\gamma)\sum_t\gamma^t\mu^{\top}P_{\pi'}^t=(d^{\pi'})^{\top}$. Hence $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_sd^{\pi'}(s)\bar a(s)$. Only the two Bellman equations were used; the telescoping proof of Section 1 is the same Neumann series read along trajectories.
(c) $P_\pi=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $r_\pi=(0,1)$, so $V^\pi=(I-\tfrac12P_\pi)^{-1}r_\pi=(0.5,\,1.5)$ and $J(\pi)=0.5$. Then $Q^\pi(0,\cdot)=(0.25,0.75)$ and $Q^\pi(1,\cdot)=(1.75,1.25)$ for (stay, switch), so $A^\pi(0,\cdot)=(-0.25,+0.25)$, $A^\pi(1,\cdot)=(+0.25,-0.25)$. $\pi'$ picks the positive-advantage action in both states: $\bar a=(0.25,0.25)$. Under $\pi'$ the chain is $0\to1\to1\to\dots$: $V^{\pi'}=(1,2)$, $J(\pi')=1$, $d^{\pi'}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, and indeed $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a\rangle=2\cdot0.25=0.5=J(\pi')-J(\pi)$; also $(I-\tfrac12P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a=(0.5,0.5)=V^{\pi'}-V^\pi$. Under $\pi$: $d^\pi=(0.75,0.25)$, and $L_\pi(\pi')=2\langle d^\pi,\bar a\rangle=0.5$ as well. The surrogate's error is $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_s(d^{\pi'}-d^\pi)(s)\,\bar a(s)$; here $\bar a$ is constant and $\sum_s(d^{\pi'}-d^\pi)(s)=0$, so the error vanishes. The surrogate is wrong only through the correlation between where the state distribution moves and where the advantage is large, which is what the bound of Section 2 controls with $\epsilon^{\pi'}$.

(c) Two states $\{0,1\}$, deterministic actions stay and switch, reward 1 per step in state 1, $\gamma=\tfrac12$, start in state 0. $\pi$ switches with probability $\tfrac12$ in both states; $\pi'$ switches in state 0 and stays in state 1. Compute $A^\pi$, $\bar a$, $d^{\pi'}$ and $d^\pi$, check the lemma, and explain why the surrogate $L_\pi(\pi')$ happens to be exact here.
solution_snippets:
Show answer
(a) $\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)Q^\pi(s,a)=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)\big[r(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V^\pi(s')\big]=r_{\pi'}(s)+\gamma(P_{\pi'}V^\pi)(s)$; subtract $V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)V^\pi(s)$.
(b) The Bellman equation of $\pi'$ is $V^{\pi'}=r_{\pi'}+\gamma P_{\pi'}V^{\pi'}$. Subtract $V^\pi$ and add and subtract $\gamma P_{\pi'}V^\pi$: $V^{\pi'}-V^\pi=\underbrace{r_{\pi'}+\gamma P_{\pi'}V^\pi-V^\pi}_{=\bar a}+\gamma P_{\pi'}(V^{\pi'}-V^\pi)$. Since $\|\gamma P_{\pi'}\|_\infty=\gamma\lt1$, $I-\gamma P_{\pi'}$ is invertible with Neumann series $\sum_t\gamma^tP_{\pi'}^t$, so $V^{\pi'}-V^\pi=(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a$. Multiply by $\mu^{\top}$: $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\mu^{\top}(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a=\sum_t\gamma^t(\mu^{\top}P_{\pi'}^t)\bar a$, and $\mu^{\top}P_{\pi'}^t$ is the law of $s_t$ under $\pi'$, so $(1-\gamma)\sum_t\gamma^t\mu^{\top}P_{\pi'}^t=(d^{\pi'})^{\top}$. Hence $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_sd^{\pi'}(s)\bar a(s)$. Only the two Bellman equations were used; the telescoping proof of Section 1 is the same Neumann series read along trajectories.
(c) $P_\pi=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $r_\pi=(0,1)$, so $V^\pi=(I-\tfrac12P_\pi)^{-1}r_\pi=(0.5,\,1.5)$ and $J(\pi)=0.5$. Then $Q^\pi(0,\cdot)=(0.25,0.75)$ and $Q^\pi(1,\cdot)=(1.75,1.25)$ for (stay, switch), so $A^\pi(0,\cdot)=(-0.25,+0.25)$, $A^\pi(1,\cdot)=(+0.25,-0.25)$. $\pi'$ picks the positive-advantage action in both states: $\bar a=(0.25,0.25)$. Under $\pi'$ the chain is $0\to1\to1\to\dots$: $V^{\pi'}=(1,2)$, $J(\pi')=1$, $d^{\pi'}=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, and indeed $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a\rangle=2\cdot0.25=0.5=J(\pi')-J(\pi)$; also $(I-\tfrac12P_{\pi'})^{-1}\bar a=(0.5,0.5)=V^{\pi'}-V^\pi$. Exercise 9.2 — When CPO is TRPO, and a second CPO step by hand

Consider the CPO subproblem $\max_xg^{ op}x$ s.t. $c+b^{ op}x\le0$, $ frac12x^{ op}Hx\le\delta$ with $H\succ0$. (a) Derive its dual function $D(\lambda, u)=\max_x\mathcal L(x,\lambda, u)$ for $\lambda\gt0$, $ u\ge0$, and show that $D$ is jointly convex. (b) Show that if the TRPO step satisfies the linearised constraint, $c+r\sqrt{2\delta/q}\le0$, then $(\lambda, u)=(\sqrt{q/(2\delta)},0)$ minimises $D$, so CPO returns the TRPO step (the claim in the theorem of Section 3). (c) Take $g=(1,\,0.4)$, $b=(0.6,\,0.8)$, $H= egin{pmatrix}2&0.5\0.5&1\end{pmatrix}$, $\delta=0.05$, $c=-0.1$, and use $H^{-1}g=(0.457,\,0.171)$, $H^{-1}b=(0.114,\,0.743)$. Compute $q,r,s$, decide the regime, compute $\lambda^\star, u^\star,x^\star$, and verify strong duality numerically.

Show answer
(a) $\mathcal L=g^{ op}x- u(c+b^{ op}x)-\lambda( frac12x^{ op}Hx-\delta)$ is strictly concave in $x$ for $\lambda\gt0$; $ abla_x\mathcal L=g- u b-\lambda Hx=0$ gives $x= rac1\lambda H^{-1}(g- u b)$, and substituting, $D(\lambda, u)= rac{1}{2\lambda}(g- u b)^{ op}H^{-1}(g- u b)- u c+\lambda\delta= rac{q-2 u r+ u^2s}{2\lambda}- u c+\lambda\delta$. With $w=H^{-1/2}(g- u b)$, affine in $ u$, the first term is $\|w\|^2/(2\lambda)$, the perspective of the convex function $ frac12\|w\|^2$; perspectives are jointly convex in $(w,\lambda)$ on $\lambda\gt0$, and composing with an affine map preserves convexity. The other two terms are linear.
(b) Let $\lambda_0=\sqrt{q/(2\delta)}\gt0$. Multiplying the hypothesis by $\lambda_0$ gives $\lambda_0c+r\le0$. First-order conditions of the convex problem $\min_{\lambda\gt0, u\ge0}D$ at $(\lambda_0,0)$: $\partial_\lambda D=- rac{q}{2\lambda_0^2}+\delta=0$, and $\partial_ u D= rac{ u s-r}{\lambda}-c=- rac{\lambda_0c+r}{\lambda_0}\ge0$, the correct sign for a minimiser on the boundary $ u=0$. For a convex differentiable function these conditions are sufficient, so $(\lambda_0,0)$ is a global minimiser, and Step 4 of the walkthrough maps it to $x^\star=H^{-1}g/\lambda_0=\sqrt{2\delta/q}\,H^{-1}g=x_{ m TRPO}$, with value $D=\sqrt{2q\delta}=g^{ op}x_{ m TRPO}$.
(c) $q=0.457+0.4\cdot0.171=0.526$, $r=0.114+0.4\cdot0.743=0.411$, $s=0.6\cdot0.114+0.8\cdot0.743=0.663$. $c^2/s=0.0151\le2\delta=0.1$: the hyperplane cuts the trust region. TRPO test: $c+r\sqrt{2\delta/q}=-0.1+0.411\cdot0.436=+0.079\gt0$, so (b) does not apply and $ u^\star\gt0$. $\lambda_a=\sqrt{ rac{q-r^2/s}{2\delta-c^2/s}}=\sqrt{ rac{0.2703}{0.0849}}=1.784$, inside $\Lambda_a=[0,\,r/|c|)=[0,\,4.11)$; $ u^\star= rac{\lambda_ac+r}{s}= rac{-0.178+0.411}{0.663}=0.352$; $x^\star= rac{1}{1.784} ig[(0.457,0.171)-0.352\,(0.114,0.743) ig]=(0.234,\,-0.050)$. Checks: $c+b^{ op}x^\star=-0.1+0.140-0.040=0$ and $ frac12x^{\star op}Hx^\star=0.050=\delta$ (both active); $g^{ op}x^\star=0.234-0.020=0.214$. Dual value: $D_a(\lambda_a)=\sqrt{(q-r^2/s)(2\delta-c^2/s)}- rac{rc}{s}=0.152+0.062=0.214$: zero duality gap. For comparison, $D_b$ at its projected minimiser $\lambda_b=\max ig(\sqrt{q/(2\delta)},\,r/|c| ig)=\max(2.29,4.11)=4.11$ is $ rac{q}{2\lambda_b}+\lambda_b\delta=0.064+0.206=0.270\gt0.214$, which confirms $\lambda^\star=\lambda_a$ (the $\Lambda_a$ case of regime 2). Enter these values in the explorer (with $H_{12}=0.5$, $H_{22}=1$) to see the step.

Exercise 9.3 — The FOCOPS policy for two actions

One state, two actions, $\pi_k=(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, advantages $A=(+1,-1)$ and cost advantages $A_c=(+2,-2)$ (both average to zero under $\pi_k$, as advantages must). Let $p=\pi^\star(a_1)$ in the closed form of Section 4. (a) Write $p$ as a function of the temperature $\lambda$ and the cost multiplier $\nu$. (b) With $\lambda=1$ and the cost constraint $\mathbb E_{\pi^\star}[A_c]\le\tilde b=0.5$, find the smallest feasible $\nu$ and the resulting $p$. (c) Compute $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi^\star\|\pi_k)$ and compare it with $\delta=0.05$. What are the exact multipliers of the two-constraint problem? (d) Repeat for $\delta=0.02$: which constraint binds now?

Show answer
(a) $\pi^\star(a)\propto\pi_k(a)\exp\big((A(a)-\nu A_c(a))/\lambda\big)$, so with $u=(1-2\nu)/\lambda$: $p=\frac{e^{u}}{e^{u}+e^{-u}}=\sigma\big(2(1-2\nu)/\lambda\big)$, $\sigma$ the logistic function (see Primer E).
(b) $\mathbb E_{\pi^\star}[A_c]=2p-2(1-p)=4p-2\le0.5\iff p\le0.625$. With $\nu=0$: $p=\sigma(2)=0.881$, violated. Equality: $2(1-2\nu)=\ln\frac{0.625}{0.375}=0.511$, so $\nu=0.372$ and $p=0.625$. The objective is $\mathbb E_{\pi^\star}[A]=2p-1=0.25$, down from $0.762$ without the cost constraint.
(c) $D_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.625\ln1.25+0.375\ln0.75=0.1395-0.1079=0.0316\le0.05$: the trust region is slack. The exact solution of the two-constraint problem is therefore $p=0.625$, with multipliers $(\lambda,\nu)=(0,\,0.5)$ by complementary slackness and stationarity of the (now linear) Lagrangian $2p-1-\nu(4p-2.5)$; the Gibbs form degenerates at $\lambda=0$. FOCOPS, which fixes the temperature at $\lambda=1$, reaches the same policy with $\nu=0.372$. With a single free parameter $p$, a fixed temperature reproduces it whenever an admissible $\nu\ge0$ makes the cost constraint tight: $p=0.625$ requires $\nu=\tfrac12-\tfrac\lambda4\ln\tfrac53$, which is non-negative only for $\lambda\le2/\ln\tfrac53\approx3.915$. For hotter temperatures the unconstrained Gibbs policy already has $p=\sigma(2/\lambda)\lt0.625$ (e.g. $0.583$ at $\lambda=6$), so $\nu=0$ and FOCOPS takes a smaller step than the exact solution. The multiplier values are not comparable across temperatures.
(d) $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p)=p\ln2p+(1-p)\ln2(1-p)$ increases for $p\gt\tfrac12$ and reaches $0.02$ at $p=0.5997$ (check: $0.6\ln1.2+0.4\ln0.8=0.0201$). Now the KL constraint binds first: $4p-2=0.399\lt0.5$ leaves the cost constraint slack, so $\nu^\star=0$, and the temperature solves $\sigma(2/\lambda)=0.5997$, i.e. $2/\lambda=\ln\frac{0.5997}{0.4003}=0.404$, $\lambda^\star\approx4.95$. It indeed minimises the dual $\lambda\delta+\lambda\ln\cosh(1/\lambda)$: the derivative $\delta+\ln\cosh(1/\lambda)-\tanh(1/\lambda)/\lambda$ vanishes there. Moral: the two multipliers take turns; FOCOPS in practice fixes $\lambda$, adapts only $\nu$, and enforces $\delta$ by rejecting states and stopping early.

With a single free parameter $p$, a fixed temperature reproduces it whenever an admissible $ u\ge0$ makes the cost constraint tight: $p=0.625$ requires $ u= frac12- frac\lambda4\ln frac53$, which is non-negative only for $\lambda\le2/\ln frac53\approx3.915$. For hotter temperatures the unconstrained Gibbs policy already has $p=\sigma(2/\lambda)\lt0.625$ (e.g. $0.583$ at $\lambda=6$), so $ u=0$ and FOCOPS takes a smaller step than the exact solution. (d) $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p)=p\ln2p+(1-p)\ln2(1-p)$ increases for $p\gt frac12$ and reaches $0.02$ at $p=0.5997$ (check: $0.6\ln1.2+0.4\ln0.8=0.0201$). items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.4 — The exact-penalty threshold behind P3O

Minimise $f(\theta)=(\theta-2)^2$ subject to $g(\theta)=\theta-1\le0$ on $\mathbb R$. (a) Find $\bar\theta$ and the KKT multiplier $\bar\lambda$. (b) For the ReLU penalty $F_\kappa(\theta)=f(\theta)+\kappa\max\{0,\theta-1\}$, find the minimiser for every $\kappa\gt0$ and the exactness threshold. (c) Compare with the quadratic penalty $f+\frac\mu2\max\{0,\theta-1\}^2$ and with IPO's barrier $f-\frac1t\log(1-\theta)$: how does the error decay, and what do the barrier's implied multipliers $-1/(t\,g(\theta_t))$ converge to? (d) Give a one-line problem in which $\kappa=\bar\lambda$ admits infeasible minimisers of the penalised problem.

Show answer
(a) The unconstrained minimiser $\theta=2$ is infeasible, so the constraint is active: $\bar\theta=1$, and stationarity $2(\bar\theta-2)+\bar\lambda=0$ gives $\bar\lambda=2$.
(b) For $\theta\le1$, $F_\kappa=(\theta-2)^2$ is decreasing. For $\theta\gt1$, $F_\kappa'(\theta)=2(\theta-2)+\kappa$ vanishes at $\theta=2-\kappa/2$. If $\kappa\lt2$ this point lies above 1 and is the minimiser, infeasible by $1-\kappa/2$ (e.g. $\kappa=1$: $\theta=1.5$). If $\kappa\ge2$, $F_\kappa$ is increasing on $\theta\gt1$ and $\bar\theta=1$ is the unique minimiser. Threshold: $\kappa\ge\bar\lambda=2$ (at $\kappa=2$ the minimiser is still unique here because $f$ is strictly convex).
(c) Quadratic penalty: for $\theta\gt1$, $2(\theta-2)+\mu(\theta-1)=0$ gives $\theta_\mu=\frac{4+\mu}{2+\mu}$, infeasible by $\frac{2}{2+\mu}$ for every finite $\mu$ ($\mu=10$: $0.167$; $\mu=100$: $0.020$). Barrier: for $\theta\lt1$, $2(\theta-2)+\frac{1}{t(1-\theta)}=0$; with $u=1-\theta$ this is $2u^2+2u=1/t$, so $u=\frac{\sqrt{1+2/t}-1}{2}\approx\frac{1}{2t}$. The iterate is strictly feasible and the objective gap is $f(\theta_t)-f(\bar\theta)=(1+u)^2-1=2u+u^2=\frac1t-u^2\le\frac1t$: exactly IPO's $m/t$ bound with $m=1$ ($t=10$: $0.098\le0.1$). The implied multiplier $\lambda_t=\frac{1}{tu}$ equals $2.10$ at $t=10$ and $2.01$ at $t=100$, converging to $\bar\lambda=2$: the barrier follows the central path. Only the ReLU penalty is exact at a finite weight, and that weight is the unknown $\bar\lambda$; hence P3O's schedule $\kappa\leftarrow\min(\rho\kappa,\kappa_{\max})$.
(d) Minimise $-\theta$ subject to $\theta\le0$: $\bar\theta=0$, $\bar\lambda=1$. With $\kappa=1$, $F(\theta)=-\theta+\max\{0,\theta\}=\max\{-\theta,0\}$ attains its minimum $0$ at every $\theta\ge0$, including every infeasible $\theta\gt0$; for $\kappa\gt1$ the minimiser $\theta=0$ is unique, for $\kappa\lt1$ there is none. This is why part (b) of the theorem in Section 4 needs $\kappa\gt\|\bar\lambda\|_\infty$.

items.label: Exercise 9.5 — Reading the Safety Gym table
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.5 — Reading the Safety Gym table

Use the SG18 table of Section 3 and the definitions of Section 7 ($d=25$, $T_{\rm ep}=1000$). (a) State in words what $\bar M_c=0.593$ for CPO means. (b) Suppose that on some task unconstrained PPO has cost rate $\rho_c^E=0.10$ (an illustrative number). Which cost rates do the SG18 averages $\bar\rho_c$ imply for PPO-Lagrangian, TRPO-Lagrangian and CPO, and which of them satisfy "the average training episode satisfied the constraint", $\rho_cT_{\rm ep}\le d$? (c) How can an algorithm have $\bar M_c\approx0$ and yet a large $\bar\rho_c$? (d) Under Safety Gym's ranking rules, which algorithm is best? (e) Why does the omission of CPO's failure predictor matter for the comparison?

Show answer
(a) At the end of training, with the per-environment ratio averaged over 18 environments and 3 seeds, CPO's excess episode cost $\max(0,J_c-25)$ was 59.3% of the excess of unconstrained PPO. Zero would mean constraint satisfaction; the Lagrangian values $0.026$ and $0.018$ are small positive violations; no uncertainty interval is supplied.
(b) Treat this as a hypothetical task whose ratios equal the reported SG18 averages; the aggregate does not determine any individual task's cost. Then $\rho_c=\bar\rho_c\,\rho_c^E$: PPO-Lagrangian $0.0245$, i.e. $24.5\le25$ per episode on average (just); TRPO-Lagrangian $0.0265$, i.e. $26.5$ (slightly above); CPO $0.0646$, i.e. $64.6$. The break-even reference would be $\rho_c^E=0.025/0.245=0.102$ for PPO-Lagrangian and $0.039$ for CPO. (Averages of ratios are not ratios of averages, so this is only an order-of-magnitude reading.)
(c) $\bar M_c$ is measured at the end of training; $\rho_c$ integrates every cost over the whole run, including early exploration before the multiplier has grown. A Lagrangian agent that starts unsafe and becomes safe late has a small $\bar M_c$ and a large $\bar\rho_c$. This is why Safety Gym proposes the cost rate as a measure of safety regret, and why later work reports safety during learning.
(d) Agents that violate the constraint rank below all agents that satisfy it, so CPO ($\bar M_c=0.593$) is last despite its return of $0.784$. Among the two approximately feasible methods, TRPO-Lagrangian has the higher return ($0.331$ vs $0.24$) but also the higher cost rate ($0.265$ vs $0.245$): neither dominates the other, and the ranking depends on how one weighs return against safety regret. Note that the two metrics even disagree on "safer": TRPO-Lagrangian has the smaller final violation but the larger cost rate.
(e) Cost shaping constrains $C^+=C+\Delta\ge C$, an algebraic upper bound when the learned bonus is nonnegative, which builds in a margin against exactly the approximation errors the report blames. Without it, an active-constraint CPO step drives the estimated cost to the limit and every optimistic estimation error becomes a violation. The fair conclusion is that CPO's worst-case bound lives on the exact surrogate problem, and its practical margin lived in the shaping.

items.label: Exercise 9.6 — Designing CDT's cost-to-go conditioning
items.source_snippet:
Exercise 9.6 — Designing CDT's cost-to-go conditioning

An offline dataset contains five trajectories with (reward return, cost return) $(10,30)$, $(8,15)$, $(6,5)$, $(5,12)$, $(3,0)$. Let $\mathrm{PF}(\kappa)=\max\{R(\tau):C(\tau)\le\kappa\}$ be the dataset's Pareto frontier. A user wants episode cost at most $\kappa=10$. (a) Which initial tokens $(R_1,C_1)$ should the CDT policy receive, and why is $R_1=9$ a bad idea? (b) After the first step the agent observes $r_1=0.5$, $c_1=1$: give the next tokens. (c) Which trajectory does CDT's relabelling (its Algorithm 1) attach to the target $(9,10)$, how are its tokens changed, and what does the policy learn from it? (d) What goes wrong if the remaining cost budget $C_t$ becomes negative during an episode?

Show answer
(a) $\mathrm{PF}(10)=6$, from $(6,5)$; the trajectories $(8,15)$ and $(5,12)$ exceed the budget. Condition on $C_1=10$ and $R_1=6$ (relabelled data may help with higher requests but give no guarantee). $R_1=9$ asks for a return that only budget-violating trajectories reach; without relabelling the transformer may be drawn towards the $(10,30)$ and $(8,15)$ behaviours, because return tokens are just inputs to a sequence model and nothing ranks the cost token above the reward token.
(b) $R_2=R_1-r_1=5.5$ and $C_2=C_1-c_1=9$ (Algorithm 2 of the paper); the new state and the executed action are appended to the context.
(c) Algorithm 1 samples a cost target $\kappa\in[c_{\min},c_{\max}]$ and a reward target $\rho$ above what the data achieve at that cost, finds $\tau^\ast=\arg\max\{R(\tau):C(\tau)\le\kappa\}$, here $(6,5)$, and appends a copy of $\tau^\ast$ whose reward-to-go tokens are shifted element-wise by $\rho-R(\tau^\ast)=+3$ and whose cost-to-go tokens are shifted by $\kappa-C(\tau^\ast)=+5$. The model thus learns to answer the infeasible request $(9,10)$ with the actions of the best safe trajectory: the cost token gets priority. CDT states as its goal a policy whose best return at threshold $\kappa$ is at least $\mathrm{PF}(\kappa)$; this is an aim supported by experiments, not a theorem.
(d) Costs are non-negative and the relabelling only adds $\kappa-C(\tau^\ast)\ge0$, so every cost-to-go token in the training data is non-negative: a negative $C_t$ is out of distribution and the model's behaviour is undefined (the sequence-model analogue of CPQ's out-of-distribution actions). Relabelling covers targets at the start of an episode, not overshoots in the middle of one; the stochastic head and entropy term reduce compounding errors but do not remove them. A hard per-episode budget needs the state augmentation of Module 8 (Sauté RL) or FISOR-style feasibility.

(c) Algorithm 1 samples a cost target $\kappa\in[c_{\min},c_{\max}]$ and a reward target $\rho$ above what the data achieve at that cost, finds $\tau^\ast=\arg\max\{R(\tau):C(\tau)\le\kappa\}$, here $(6,5)$, and appends a copy of $\tau^\ast$ whose reward-to-go tokens are shifted element-wise by $\rho-R(\tau^\ast)=+3$ and whose cost-to-go tokens are shifted by $\kappa-C(\tau^\ast)=+5$. The model thus learns to answer the infeasible request $(9,10)$ with the actions of the best safe trajectory: the cost token gets priority. CDT states as its goal a policy whose best return at threshold $\kappa$ is at least $\mathrm{PF}(\kappa)$; this is an aim supported by experiments, not a theorem.
(d) Costs are non-negative and the relabelling only adds $\kappa-C(\tau^\ast)\ge0$, so every cost-to-go token in the training data is non-negative: a negative $C_t$ is out of distribution and the model's behaviour is undefined (the sequence-model analogue of CPQ's out-of-distribution actions). Relabelling covers targets at the start of an episode, not overshoots in the middle of one; the stochastic head and entropy term reduce compounding errors but do not remove them. A hard per-episode budget needs the state augmentation of Module 8 (Sauté RL) or FISOR-style feasibility.

items.label: Module 8 solved CMDPs in the space of occupancy measures, where the problem is a linear program and duality is exact (Mo
items.source_snippet: Module 8 solved CMDPs in the space of occupancy measures, where the problem is a linear program and duality is exact (Module 8). Deep safe RL cannot work there: the policy is a network $\pi_\theta$ (see Primer E), the state space is continuous, and every quantity has to be estimated from trajectories of the current policy. Policy search therefore moves in small steps $\pi_k\to\pi_{k+1}$, and every step must answer two questions using data of $\pi_k$ only: how much will the return improve, and how much will the cost grow? This module is built on one identity that answers both exactly but is not computable (the performance difference lemma), one inequality that answers them conservatively given a valid global advantage bound (the trust-region bound behind CPO), and the family of algorithms that optimise the resulting surrogate problem.

items.source_snippet:
Reference — notation changes across papers
Caveat — Notation clashes on this page
We keep the letters of the original papers because every implementation uses them. (i) In CPO, $c$ without arguments is the scalar constraint value $J_c(\pi_k)-d$, while $c(s,a)$ is the cost function; likewise $q,r,s$ are scalars, not the reward $r(s,a)$ or a state $s$. (ii) Multipliers: in CPO, PCPO and FOCOPS, $\lambda$ multiplies the trust-region (KL) constraint and $\nu$ the cost constraint; CVPO writes $\eta$ for the KL multiplier and $\lambda$ for the cost multiplier; LAMBDA, SafeDreamer, COptiDICE and Module 8 use $\lambda$ for the cost multiplier, and COptiDICE's $\nu(s)$ is a Bellman-flow multiplier (a value function). P3O writes $\kappa$ for its penalty factor, whereas CDT, DSRL, OASIS and O3SRL (Section 6) write $\kappa$ for the cost threshold, our $d$. (iii) $\delta$ is the trust-region radius here, but a failure probability in ActSafe and SOOPER. (iv) $\beta$ is C-TRPO's barrier weight and CUP's penalty coefficient; GP confidence scalings are written $\beta_n$ as in Module 3. (v) $\Gamma_N$ is the maximum information gain of Module 3 (written $\gamma_t$ there; here $\gamma$ is the discount). (vi) FISOR's constraint function $h$ marks safe states by $h\le0$ and takes a maximum over time, the opposite sign of the barrier convention $h\ge0$ of the global notation and of the safety margin $l\ge0$ developed later (see Module 10).

items.label: Proof sketch — Telescoping the old advantage along new trajectories Step 1 (advantage as a TD residual). Along a traject
items.source_snippet:
Proof sketch — Telescoping the old advantage along new trajectories

Step 1 (advantage as a TD residual). Along a trajectory of $\pi'$, the next state has the conditional law $P(\cdot\mid s_t,a_t)$ no matter which policy chose $a_t$. Since $Q^\pi(s_t,a_t)=\mathbb E[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})\mid s_t,a_t]$, the tower property gives (see Primer C)

$$\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi'}\big[A^\pi(s_t,a_t)\big]=\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi'}\big[r(s_t,a_t)+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})-V^\pi(s_t)\big].$$

Step 2 (telescoping). Multiply by $\gamma^t$ and sum up to a horizon $T$; the value terms cancel pairwise:

$$\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^t\big(r_t+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1})-V^\pi(s_t)\big)=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^tr_t+\gamma^TV^\pi(s_T)-V^\pi(s_0).$$

Step 3 (the tail vanishes). Take expectations in Step 2 (using Step 1 on the left) and let $T\to\infty$. No convergence theorem is needed, because every tail is small on every trajectory: $|\gamma^TV^\pi(s_T)|\le\gamma^Tr_{\max}/(1-\gamma)$, and since $|r|\le r_{\max}$ and $|A^\pi|\le|Q^\pi|+|V^\pi|\le2r_{\max}/(1-\gamma)$, the parts of $\sum_t\gamma^tr_t$ and $\sum_t\gamma^tA^\pi(s_t,a_t)$ after time $T$ are at most $r_{\max}\gamma^T/(1-\gamma)$ and $2r_{\max}\gamma^T/(1-\gamma)^2$ in absolute value (geometric series). A bound that holds for every trajectory also bounds the expectation, and all three bounds tend to $0$:

$$\mathbb E_{\tau\sim\pi'}\Big[\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tA^\pi(s_t,a_t)\Big]=J(\pi')-\mathbb E_{s_0\sim\mu}\big[V^\pi(s_0)\big]=J(\pi')-J(\pi).$$

Step 4 (occupancy form). Write the expectation state by state: $\sum_t\gamma^t\,\mathbb E[A^\pi(s_t,a_t)]=\sum_s\big(\sum_t\gamma^t\mathbb P(s_t=s\mid\pi')\big)\sum_a\pi'(a\mid s)A^\pi(s,a)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{s\sim d^{\pi'},a\sim\pi'}[A^\pi(s,a)]$. $\square$

Corollary (policy improvement theorem, Primer E). If $\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi'}[A^\pi(s,a)]\ge0$ at every state, every term of the expectation is non-negative, so $J(\pi')\ge J(\pi)$. The greedy policy of policy iteration satisfies this condition. Equality $J(\pi')=J(\pi)$ for one $\mu$ does not prove optimality ($\mu$ may never reach the states where improvement is possible); the optimality test is statewise, $\max_aQ^\pi(s,a)=V^\pi(s)$ for every $s$.

items.source_snippet:
Derivation — The surrogate has the right gradient (and the policy gradient theorem falls out)

Let $\pi_ heta$ be differentiable in $ heta$ and $\pi_k=\pi_{ heta_k}$. For finite MDPs write distributions as column vectors and let $[P_\pi]_{s',s}=\sum_aP(s'\mid s,a)\pi(a\mid s)$ (each column sums to one; Exercise 9.1 uses the transpose, acting on value vectors). The state distribution at time $t$ is $p_t=P_\pi^t\mu$, so $d^\pi=(1-\gamma)\sum_t\gamma^tP_\pi^t\mu$ satisfies $d^\pi=(1-\gamma)\mu+\gamma P_\pi d^\pi$, i.e. $d^{\pi_ heta}=(1-\gamma)(I-\gamma P_{\pi_ heta})^{-1}\mu$ (Section 2 shows the inverse exists). This is a differentiable function of $ heta$, because $P_{\pi_ heta}$ is linear in the probabilities $\pi_ heta$ and matrix inversion is differentiable. Apply the lemma with $\pi=\pi_k$, $\pi'=\pi_ heta$ and write it as a double sum:

$$J(\pi_ heta)-J(\pi_k)= rac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_s d^{\pi_ heta}(s)\sum_a\pi_ heta(a\mid s)\,A^{\pi_k}(s,a).$$

Differentiate at $ heta= heta_k$ with the product rule (see Primer B). The term in which $d^{\pi_ heta}$ is differentiated is multiplied by $\sum_a\pi_k(a\mid s)A^{\pi_k}(s,a)=\sum_a\pi_k(a\mid s)Q^{\pi_k}(s,a)-V^{\pi_k}(s)=0$ (the advantage has zero mean under its own policy, by the definition of $V^{\pi_k}$), so it vanishes:

$$ abla_ heta J(\pi_ heta) ig|_{ heta_k}= rac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_sd^{\pi_k}(s)\sum_a abla_ heta\pi_ heta(a\mid s) ig|_{ heta_k}A^{\pi_k}(s,a)= abla_ heta L_{\pi_k}(\pi_ heta) ig|_{ heta_k}.$$

The error is second order because of its product form: in the key equation above, $J(\pi_ heta)-J(\pi_k)-L_{\pi_k}(\pi_ heta)= rac{1}{1-\gamma}\sum_s ig(d^{\pi_ heta}(s)-d^{\pi_k}(s) ig) ar a(s)$ with $ ar a(s)=\sum_a ig(\pi_ heta(a\mid s)-\pi_k(a\mid s) ig)A^{\pi_k}(s,a)$ (zero mean again). Differentiability at $ heta_k$ makes each factor $O(\|x\|)$ (at most a constant times $\|x\|$) for small $x= heta- heta_k$, so the product is $O(\|x\|^2)$ (Primer 0).

Using $ abla\pi=\pi abla\log\pi$ gives the policy gradient theorem, $ abla_ heta J= rac{1}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{s\sim d^{\pi_k},a\sim\pi_k}[ abla_ heta\log\pi_ heta(a\mid s)A^{\pi_k}(s,a)]$. So the surrogate agrees with the true objective to first order: the vector $g= abla_ heta L_{\pi_k}(\pi_ heta)|_{ heta_k}$ that CPO uses is the policy gradient. The same argument gives $b= abla_ heta L_{c,\pi_k}(\pi_ heta)|_{ heta_k}= abla_ heta J_c(\pi_ heta)|_{ heta_k}$. The remaining error is second order: how far the state distribution drifts, which is what Section 2 bounds.

items.label: Why it matters A safety constraint $J_c(\pi_{k+1})\le d$ is a statement about the states the next policy will visit. Bef
items.source_snippet:
Why it matters
A safety constraint $J_c(\pi_{k+1})\le d$ is a statement about the states the next policy will visit. Before deploying $\pi_{k+1}$ we cannot sample them, and off-policy evaluation of every candidate (see Primer E) is unreliable in high dimensions. The whole trust-region line (TRPO, CPO, PCPO, CUP, C-TRPO) is a way to replace $d^{\pi_{k+1}}$ by $d^{\pi_k}$ and pay a controlled price for it.

items.source_snippet:
Pitfall — Normalisation conventions change the constants
With the normalised occupancy $d^\pi$ the lemma carries the factor $1/(1-\gamma)$; with the unnormalised visitation $\tilde\rho_\pi(s)=\sum_t\gamma^t\mathbb P(s_t=s)$ used by Schulman et al., ICML 2015 it does not. Some papers also normalise values, e.g. COptiDICE uses $V_R(\pi)=\mathbb E_{(s,a)\sim d^\pi}[R]=(1-\gamma)J(\pi)$. Constants such as $4\epsilon\gamma/(1-\gamma)^2$ move by factors of $1-\gamma$ when conventions are mixed, so always check which occupancy a bound uses before comparing it with another.

section.title: 2. Trust-Region Bounds for Return and Cost

items.source_snippet:
Derivation — From the performance difference lemma to the bound (Achiam et al., App. 10.1)

Step 1 (vector form). With $\bar a(s)=\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi'}[A^\pi(s,a)]$, the lemma reads $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a\rangle$.

Step 2 (add and subtract the old distribution). $\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a\rangle=\langle d^{\pi},\bar a\rangle+\langle d^{\pi'}-d^\pi,\bar a\rangle$. The first term is exactly $(1-\gamma)L_\pi(\pi')$.

Step 3 (Hölder with $p=1$, $q=\infty$; Primer A). $|\langle d^{\pi'}-d^\pi,\bar a\rangle|\le\sum_s|d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s)|\,|\bar a(s)|\le\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\,\|\bar a\|_\infty=\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\,\epsilon^{\pi'}$ (bound each $|\bar a(s)|$ by the largest one). (Achiam et al. remark that other Hölder pairs could give other bounds.)

Step 4 (how far can the state distribution drift?). Let $P_\pi(s'\mid s)=\sum_aP(s'\mid s,a)\pi(a\mid s)$, a column-stochastic matrix, so that $d^\pi=(1-\gamma)(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}\mu$. Put $G=(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}$, $\bar G=(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}$, $\Delta=P_{\pi'}-P_\pi$. Then $G^{-1}-\bar G^{-1}=\gamma\Delta$; multiplying by $\bar G$ on the left and $G$ on the right gives the resolvent identity $\bar G-G=\gamma\bar G\Delta G$, hence

$$d^{\pi'}-d^\pi=(1-\gamma)(\bar G-G)\mu=\gamma\,\bar G\,\Delta\,d^\pi .$$

The induced 1-norm of a matrix is its maximal absolute column sum, so a column-stochastic matrix has $\|P_{\pi'}\|_1=1$ (Primer A). With $A=\gamma P_{\pi'}$ and $S_N=I+A+\cdots+A^N$, multiplying out gives $(I-A)S_N=I-A^{N+1}$, and $\|A^{N+1}\|_1\le\gamma^{N+1}\to0$; so $I-A$ is invertible with the matrix geometric (Neumann) series $\bar G=\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tP_{\pi'}^t$ (Primer 0). By the triangle inequality and submultiplicativity, $\|\bar G\|_1\le\sum_t\gamma^t\|P_{\pi'}\|_1^t=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$. And

$$\begin{aligned}\|\Delta d^\pi\|_1&=\sum_{s'}\Big|\sum_{s,a}P(s'\mid s,a)\big(\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)\big)d^\pi(s)\Big|\\ &\le\sum_{s,a}\big|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)\big|d^\pi(s)=2\,\mathbb E_{s\sim d^\pi}\big[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]\big],\end{aligned}$$

where $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)=1$ was used after the triangle inequality. Together (Lemma 3 of the paper): $\ \|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\le\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\,\mathbb E_{s\sim d^\pi}\big[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]\big]$.

Step 5 (assemble). $J(\pi')-J(\pi)\ge\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\big(\langle d^\pi,\bar a\rangle-\frac{2\gamma\epsilon^{\pi'}}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{d^\pi}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}]\big)$, which is the stated lower bound. The cost bound uses the other side of Hölder, $\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a_c\rangle\le\langle d^\pi,\bar a_c\rangle+\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\epsilon_c^{\pi'}$. $\square$

TRPO's bound is a corollary. Since $\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)A^\pi(s,a)=0$, $\ |\bar a(s)|=|\sum_a(\pi'-\pi)(a\mid s)A^\pi(s,a)|\le2D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon=\max_{s,a}|A^\pi(s,a)|$. With $\alpha=\max_sD_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]$ this gives $\epsilon^{\pi'}\le2\alpha\epsilon$ and $\mathbb E_{d^\pi}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}]\le\alpha$, so the penalty is at most $\frac{4\epsilon\gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}\alpha^2$: the total-variation form of Theorem 1 of Schulman et al., ICML 2015, whose KL form then uses $\alpha^2\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}$ and $C=4\epsilon\gamma/(1-\gamma)^2$. items.plain_text: Derivation — From the performance difference lemma to the bound (Achiam et al., App. 10.1) Step 1 (vector form). With $\bar a(s)=\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi'}[A^\pi(s,a)]$, the lemma reads $J(\pi')-J(\pi)=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a\rangle$. Step 2 (add and subtract the old distribution). $\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a\rangle=\langle d^{\pi},\bar a\rangle+\langle d^{\pi'}-d^\pi,\bar a\rangle$. The first term is exactly $(1-\gamma)L_\pi(\pi')$. Step 3 (Hölder with $p=1$, $q=\infty$; Primer A). $|\langle d^{\pi'}-d^\pi,\bar a\rangle|\le\sum_s|d^{\pi'}(s)-d^\pi(s)|\,|\bar a(s)|\le\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\,\|\bar a\|_\infty=\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\,\epsilon^{\pi'}$ (bound each $|\bar a(s)|$ by the largest one). (Achiam et al. remark that other Hölder pairs could give other bounds.) Step 4 (how far can the state distribution drift?). Let $P_\pi(s'\mid s)=\sum_aP(s'\mid s,a)\pi(a\mid s)$, a column-stochastic matrix, so that $d^\pi=(1-\gamma)(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}\mu$. Put $G=(I-\gamma P_\pi)^{-1}$, $\bar G=(I-\gamma P_{\pi'})^{-1}$, $\Delta=P_{\pi'}-P_\pi$. Then $G^{-1}-\bar G^{-1}=\gamma\Delta$; multiplying by $\bar G$ on the left and $G$ on the right gives the resolvent identity $\bar G-G=\gamma\bar G\Delta G$, hence $$d^{\pi'}-d^\pi=(1-\gamma)(\bar G-G)\mu=\gamma\,\bar G\,\Delta\,d^\pi .$$ The induced 1-norm of a matrix is its maximal absolute column sum, so a column-stochastic matrix has $\|P_{\pi'}\|_1=1$ (Primer A). With $A=\gamma P_{\pi'}$ and $S_N=I+A+\cdots+A^N$, multiplying out gives $(I-A)S_N=I-A^{N+1}$, and $\|A^{N+1}\|_1\le\gamma^{N+1}\to0$; so $I-A$ is invertible with the matrix geometric (Neumann) series $\bar G=\sum_{t\ge0}\gamma^tP_{\pi'}^t$ (Primer 0). By the triangle inequality and submultiplicativity, $\|\bar G\|_1\le\sum_t\gamma^t\|P_{\pi'}\|_1^t=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}$. And $$\begin{aligned}\|\Delta d^\pi\|_1&=\sum_{s'}\Big|\sum_{s,a}P(s'\mid s,a)\big(\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)\big)d^\pi(s)\Big|\\ &\le\sum_{s,a}\big|\pi'(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)\big|d^\pi(s)=2\,\mathbb E_{s\sim d^\pi}\big[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]\big],\end{aligned}$$ where $\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)=1$ was used after the triangle inequality. Together (Lemma 3 of the paper): $\ \|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\le\frac{2\gamma}{1-\gamma}\,\mathbb E_{s\sim d^\pi}\big[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]\big]$. Step 5 (assemble). $J(\pi')-J(\pi)\ge\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\big(\langle d^\pi,\bar a\rangle-\frac{2\gamma\epsilon^{\pi'}}{1-\gamma}\mathbb E_{d^\pi}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}]\big)$, which is the stated lower bound. The cost bound uses the other side of Hölder, $\langle d^{\pi'},\bar a_c\rangle\le\langle d^\pi,\bar a_c\rangle+\|d^{\pi'}-d^\pi\|_1\epsilon_c^{\pi'}$. $\square$ TRPO's bound is a corollary. Since $\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)A^\pi(s,a)=0$, $\ |\bar a(s)|=|\sum_a(\pi'-\pi)(a\mid s)A^\pi(s,a)|\le2D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon=\max_{s,a}|A^\pi(s,a)|$. With $\alpha=\max_sD_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]$ this gives $\epsilon^{\pi'}\le2\alpha\epsilon$ and $\mathbb E_{d^\pi}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}]\le\alpha$, so the penalty is at most $\frac{4\epsilon\gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}\alpha^2$: the total-variation form of Theorem 1 of Schulman et al., ICML 2015, whose KL form then uses $\alpha^2\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}^{\max}$ and $C=4\epsilon\gamma/(1-\gamma)^2$. CPO's version is tighter because it keeps the average over $d^\pi$ instead of the maximum over states.

items.source_snippet:
Caveat — What these guarantees do and do not say
(1) They are approximate constraint satisfaction: each exact step may overshoot the budget, and nothing prevents overshoots from accumulating if later steps do not recover. (2) The constant is large: with $\gamma=0.99$, $\delta=0.01$ and $\epsilon_c^{\pi_{k+1}}=0.05$, the allowed overshoot is $\sqrt{0.02}\cdot0.99\cdot0.05/10^{-4}\approx70$ cost units, nearly three times Safety Gym's budget $d=25$. (3) They hold for the exact update (10) over the policy class; the practical CPO step linearises, uses a quadratic model of the KL, and plugs in noisy estimates of $c=J_c(\pi_k)-d$, $A^{\pi_k}$ and $A_c^{\pi_k}$, none of which is covered. (4) TRPO's own theory was stated with the maximal KL while its algorithm constrained the mean KL; CPO's Theorem 1 removes that gap, but not the others. Do not read "CPO guarantees constraint satisfaction" into these propositions.

items.label: Key insight — Why $d^{\pi}$ instead of $d^{\pi'}$ is the whole point Every term in the update (objective, cost constrain

section.title: 2. Trust-Region Bounds for Return and Cost

items.source_snippet:
Key insight — Why $d^{\pi}$ instead of $d^{\pi'}$ is the whole point
Every term in the update (objective, cost constraint, trust region) is an expectation over $s\sim d^{\pi_k}$, i.e. over states in the batch just collected, with the new policy entering only through the importance ratio $\pi'(a\mid s)/\pi_k(a\mid s)$. The optimisation over $\pi'$ therefore needs no new rollouts and no off-policy evaluation. The price is the penalty term, and a trust region of radius $\delta$ is simply the cheapest way to keep that penalty small without computing it. What the batch makes computable is the update, not the certificate: the bound also needs $\epsilon^{\pi'}$, a maximum over all states, and the largest value seen in a finite batch is not a valid bound on it.

section.title: 2. Trust-Region Bounds for Return and Cost

items.source_snippet: The explorer evaluates everything exactly (linear solves, no sampling) on a three-state corridor: states $0,1,2$, action "right" moves right with probability $0.8$ and stays otherwise, "left" moves left likewise (a move beyond either end leaves the state unchanged), reward $1$ per step in state $2$, start in state $0$. The old policy goes right with probability $p$; the new policy is the mixture $\pi'=(1-\alpha)\pi+\alpha\,\pi_{\rm greedy}$ towards the greedy policy of $Q^\pi$, the conservative-policy-iteration update of Kakade and Langford. Along this path $\epsilon^{\pi'}$ and $\mathbb E_{d^\pi}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}]$ are both linear in $\alpha$, so the CPO lower bound is a concave quadratic $X\alpha-Y\alpha^2$. For $X,Y\gt0$, every $0\lt\alpha\le1$ with $\alpha\lt X/Y$ is certified to improve the return. Because the mixture weight is confined to $[0,1]$, the step with the largest guaranteed improvement is $\alpha^\star=\min\{1,X/(2Y)\}$, with guaranteed improvement $X\alpha^\star-Y(\alpha^\star)^2$; this equals $X^2/(4Y)$ only when the vertex $X/(2Y)\le1$ (at $\gamma=0.3$, $p=0.95$ the vertex is $X/(2Y)\approx4.43$, so $\alpha^\star=1$).

items.source_snippet:
Derivation — The coefficients $X$ and $Y$ of the explorer's curves

Write $\pi_g$ for the greedy policy and $\pi'=(1-\alpha)\pi+\alpha\pi_g$. Because the old policy's advantage has zero mean, $\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi'}A^\pi(s,a)=\alpha\,\mathbb E_{a\sim\pi_g}A^\pi(s,a)$, and $D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)[s]=\tfrac12\sum_a\alpha|\pi_g(a\mid s)-\pi(a\mid s)|=\alpha D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_g\|\pi)[s]$. Hence $L_\pi(\pi')=\alpha X$ with $X=L_\pi(\pi_g)$, $\epsilon^{\pi'}=\alpha e$ with $e=\max_s|\mathbb E_{\pi_g}A^\pi(s,a)|$, and $\mathbb E_{d^\pi}[D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi'\|\pi)]=\alpha v$ with $v=\mathbb E_{d^\pi}D_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_g\|\pi)$. Substituting into the CPO bound, the penalty is $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\cdot\frac{2\gamma\,\alpha e}{1-\gamma}\cdot\alpha v=Y\alpha^2$ with $Y=\frac{2\gamma ev}{(1-\gamma)^2}$. The TRPO-type bound replaces $e$ and $v$ by maxima and gives $Y_T=\frac{4\gamma\max_{s,a}|A^\pi(s,a)|\,[\max_sD_{\mathrm{TV}}(\pi_g\|\pi)]^2}{(1-\gamma)^2}$.

items.source_snippet: Applying the two bounds (in their KL form) to the objective and to the cost gives an update that maximises the surrogate minus a penalty proportional to $\sqrt{\bar D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi\|\pi_k)}$, subject to the cost surrogate plus such a penalty staying below $d$, with coefficients read off the corollaries. Solved exactly from a feasible $\pi_0$, it yields monotonically non-decreasing returns and feasible iterates. Achiam et al. note that the penalties are so steep for $\gamma$ near 1 that the steps become tiny, and replace them by a trust region, exactly as TRPO did.

items.source_snippet:
Derivation — Distance to the hyperplane and the three regimes

Write $b^\top x=(H^{-1/2}b)^\top(H^{1/2}x)$ with the matrix square roots of Primer A. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $(b^\top x)^2\le(b^\top H^{-1}b)(x^\top Hx)=s\,x^\top Hx$. On the hyperplane $b^\top x=-c$ this says $\tfrac12x^\top Hx\ge c^2/(2s)$, with equality at $x=-cH^{-1}b/s$ (substitute: $b^\top x=-c$ and $x^\top Hx=c^2/s$). On the trust region $\tfrac12x^\top Hx\le\delta$ the same inequality gives $|b^\top x|\le\sqrt{2\delta s}$, and both ends are attained, at $x=\pm\sqrt{2\delta/s}\,H^{-1}b$. The constraint asks $b^\top x\le-c$. If $-c\ge\sqrt{2\delta s}$ ($c\lt0$ and $c^2/s\ge2\delta$) every point of the trust region satisfies it; if $-c\lt-\sqrt{2\delta s}$ ($c\gt0$ and $c^2/s\gt2\delta$) none does; otherwise the hyperplane cuts the trust region.

items.source_snippet:
Pitfall — Two sign conventions for the same formula
Appendix 10.2 of the CPO paper states the closed form for the minimisation problem $\min_xg^{\top}x$ s.t. $b^{\top}x+c\le0$, $x^{\top}Hx\le\delta$: there $g$ is the gradient of a loss and the trust region has no factor $\tfrac12$. Converting to Eq. (11) requires $g\mapsto-g$ (so $r\mapsto-r$) and $\delta\mapsto2\delta$, which turns the appendix formulas $\nu^\star=((\lambda c-r)/s)_+$, $\lambda_b=\sqrt{q/\delta}$, $\Lambda_a=\{\lambda c-r\gt0\}$ into the ones above. Both are correct in their own convention; code that mixes them (loss gradient in one place, reward gradient in another) computes the wrong multiplier without any error message. The paper itself mixes them once: its main-text dual (12) ends in $-\lambda\delta/2$, the appendix's trust-region term, whereas with the $\tfrac12x^{\top}Hx\le\delta$ of Eq. (11) the term is $-\lambda\delta$ (Step 4 of the walkthrough; $D_b(\lambda)=\frac{q}{2\lambda}+\lambda\delta$ is then minimised at $\sqrt{q/(2\delta)}$, the TRPO multiplier). The explorer below checks the maximisation-form closed form against a brute-force search at every slider move.

items.label: Background — Conjugate gradientsConjugate gradients (CG) solves $Hv=g$ for symmetric positive definite $H$ by minimising
items.source_snippet:
Background — Conjugate gradients

Conjugate gradients (CG) solves $Hv=g$ for symmetric positive definite $H$ by minimising the quadratic $\tfrac12v^\top Hv-g^\top v$ (whose minimiser is $H^{-1}g$) over a growing sequence of search directions, using only products $Hv$. In exact arithmetic it finishes after at most $n$ steps; in practice it is stopped after a few, so the result is an approximate solve, controlled by the residual $g-Hv$: if $H\succeq mI$ with $m\gt0$, then $\|v-H^{-1}g\|_2=\|H^{-1}(Hv-g)\|_2\le\|g-Hv\|_2/m$. Example: $H=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)$, $g=(2,1)$ has solution $(1,1)$; the iterate $(0.9,1)$ has residual $(0.2,0)$ and error $0.1\le0.2/1$. Poor conditioning (widely separated eigenvalues) slows convergence. CPO runs CG twice, for $g$ and for $b$.

items.label: The advantages come from generalised advantage estimation (GAE). With a fitted value function $V$ (the critic) and TD re
items.source_snippet: The advantages come from generalised advantage estimation (GAE). With a fitted value function $V$ (the critic) and TD residuals $\delta_t^r=r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)$ (Primer E), a rollout $t=0,\dots,L-1$ gives $\hat A_t=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1-t}(\gamma\lambda^{\rm GAE})^\ell\delta_{t+\ell}^r$; replace $r,V$ by $c,V_c$ for the cost. At a genuine terminal state the remaining value is zero; at a truncated rollout one bootstraps from the critic. Smaller $\lambda^{\rm GAE}$ looks fewer steps ahead, which usually lowers variance but increases the dependence on critic error.

items.label: Algorithm 1: CPO, one constraint (Achiam et al. 2017, Alg. 1 with the details of Sec. 6 and App. 10.3; line-search modes
items.source_snippet:
Algorithm 1: CPO, one constraint (Achiam et al. 2017, Alg. 1 with the details of Sec. 6 and App. 10.3; line-search modes as in the authors' reference code)
  1. Input: initial policy $\pi_{\theta_0}$, trust-region radius $\delta$, backtracking factors $\omega^j$ with $\omega\in(0,1)$, $j=0,\dots,J$.
  2. for $k=0,1,2,\dots$ do
  3. Sample trajectories with $\pi_k$; estimate $\hat A$ and $\hat A_c$ with GAE (separate $\lambda^{\rm GAE}$ for costs) and $\hat c=\hat J_c(\pi_k)-d$.
  4. Form $\hat g,\hat b$ and the Fisher–vector product $v\mapsto\hat Hv$ (a Hessian–vector product, Primer B) // never build $H$ itself
  5. Conjugate gradient: $v_g\approx\hat H^{-1}\hat g$, $v_b\approx\hat H^{-1}\hat b$; then $q=\hat g^{\top}v_g$, $r=\hat g^{\top}v_b$, $s=\hat b^{\top}v_b$.
  6. after handling the degeneracies above, if the subproblem is strictly feasible: solve the dual in closed form for $(\lambda^\star,\nu^\star)$; $x^\star=(v_g-\nu^\star v_b)/\lambda^\star$ when $\lambda^\star\gt0$; otherwise use the minimum-norm chord point above.
  7. else: $x^\star=-\sqrt{2\delta/s}\;v_b$ // recovery (at a tangency, the only feasible point)
  8. Backtracking line search over $\theta_j=\theta_k+\omega^jx^\star$, $j=0,\dots,J$: accept the first $\theta_j$ whose sample estimates pass the test of the current mode:
  9. normal ($\hat c\le0$): the surrogate return improves, mean KL $\le\delta$, and the cost surrogate stays within budget, $\hat c+\hat L_{c,\pi_k}(\pi_{\theta_j})\le0$ (the constraints of (10));
  10. recovery ($\hat c\gt0$): mean KL $\le\delta$ and the cost surrogate does not increase, $\hat L_{c,\pi_k}(\pi_{\theta_j})\le0$; no return test // the budget may be out of reach, and shrinking the step only raises the cost
  11. if no $j\le J$ passes: normal mode rejects the step ($\theta\leftarrow\theta_k$); the reference code keeps its smallest recovery step (an alternative is to revert to the last feasible iterate)
  12. $\theta_{k+1}\leftarrow\theta$; refit the reward and cost value networks.

items.source_snippet: Conjugate gradients. $H$ has $n^2$ entries for $n$ network parameters, so it is never formed. CG needs only products $Hv=\nabla_\theta\big((\nabla_\theta\bar D_{\mathrm{KL}})^{\top}v\big)$ (evaluated at $\theta_k$ with $v$ held fixed; damping uses $Hv+\epsilon v$), two backward passes each, and a handful of iterations (TRPO's standard is about 10). CPO needs two solves, $H^{-1}g$ and $H^{-1}b$; everything else is scalar algebra on $q,r,s,c,\delta$. Line search. The linearisation is only locally valid, so the proposed step is shrunk until the sampled KL and cost surrogate are acceptable; this is the only place where the non-linearised problem (10) is consulted. The paper's Algorithm 1 asks the line search to enforce the constraints of (10) in every case. That is impossible when $\hat c\gt0$ and the budget is out of reach within the trust region: every backtracked recovery step is still infeasible, and shorter steps are worse. The authors' code (jachiam/cpo; defaults $\omega=0.8$, at most 15 trials) therefore checks a threshold $\max(d-\hat J_c(\pi_k),0)$ on the change of the cost surrogate: the budget in normal mode, "no increase" in recovery mode, where the return test is also dropped.

items.label: Cost shaping and the failure predictor. Because of the approximations between the original CMDP problem and the practica
items.source_snippet: Cost shaping and the failure predictor. Because of the approximations between the original CMDP problem and the practical step, Achiam et al. build in a factor of safety: they constrain an upper bound $C^+=C+\Delta$ of the cost (their Eq. 15), where the bonus $\Delta$ is a weighted output of a learned failure predictor $P_\phi(s\to U)$, a small network estimating the probability of entering an unsafe state within the next $T$ steps (horizon $T=5$ or $20$; weight $1$, or $0.01$ on Ant-Gather; no bonus on Point-Gather). Their appendix also reports that for high-dimensional robots the cost advantages had to be computed with $\lambda^{\rm GAE}_C\lt1$ (0.5): undiscounted cost advantages overestimated the constraint gradient and produced unsafe steps. In their experiments CPO drove the constraint value "almost directly to the limit", i.e. it operates on the boundary, where any estimation error becomes a violation; the shaping bonus is the margin.

items.label: Caveat — Reading the contradiction fairly Three qualifications, all stated in the Safety Gym report itself: the benchmar
items.source_snippet:
Caveat — Reading the contradiction fairly
Three qualifications, all stated in the Safety Gym report itself: the benchmark implementation of CPO omits the learned failure predictor used for cost shaping; hyperparameters were hand-tuned per algorithm class and "should not be viewed as indicative of the best-possible performance"; and the environments are harder than CPO's original Circle and Gather tasks. The mechanism behind the result is general: a method that places an active-constraint step exactly on an estimated constraint surface inherits every estimation error as a violation, whereas a multiplier that integrates the violation over time (Module 8) corrects such errors, at the price of overshoot and oscillation. Later benchmarks agree only in part: CPO is again unsafe at the last iterate in C-TRPO's comparison, but Safety-Gymnasium finds Lagrangian methods oscillating more than projection-based ones, and under zero-cost limits CPO tends to be safe but low in reward (SB-TRPO, preprint). CPO's high normalised return is not a win under Safety Gym's own ranking rule, which ranks every constraint-violating agent below every constraint-satisfying one.

items.source_snippet:
Derivation — The projection step from the KKT conditions

The linearised projection solves $\min_x\tfrac12(x-x_{\rm TRPO})^\top L(x-x_{\rm TRPO})$ subject to $c+b^\top x\le0$, with $L\succ0$. Stationarity of the Lagrangian with multiplier $\mu\ge0$ gives $L(x-x_{\rm TRPO})+\mu b=0$, i.e. $x=x_{\rm TRPO}-\mu L^{-1}b$. If $x_{\rm TRPO}$ already satisfies the constraint, $\mu=0$. Otherwise the constraint is active: substituting into $c+b^\top x=0$ gives $c+b^\top x_{\rm TRPO}-\mu\,b^\top L^{-1}b=0$, so $\mu=(c+b^\top x_{\rm TRPO})/(b^\top L^{-1}b)$. Both cases together are the $(\cdot)_+$ formula, and $b^\top x_{\rm TRPO}=\sqrt{2\delta/q}\,r$.

items.source_snippet:
Derivation — The exact result in the quadratic model: where does the projected step land?

Take $L=H$ and suppose the projection is active. Let $\beta:=b^{\top}x_{\rm TRPO}=\sqrt{2\delta/q}\,r$, so $\mu=(c+\beta)/s$ and $x_P=x_{\rm TRPO}-\mu H^{-1}b$. Expanding the quadratic and using $\tfrac12x_{\rm TRPO}^{\top}Hx_{\rm TRPO}=\delta$, $b^{\top}H^{-1}b=s$:

$$\tfrac12x_P^{\top}Hx_P=\delta-\mu\beta+\tfrac12\mu^2s=\delta-\frac{(c+\beta)\beta}{s}+\frac{(c+\beta)^2}{2s}=\delta+\frac{c^2-\beta^2}{2s}.$$

Two consequences. (i) Feasible $\pi_k$ ($c\le0$). The projection is active only if $c+\beta\gt0$, i.e. $\beta\gt-c\ge0$, so $\beta^2\gt c^2$ and $\tfrac12x_P^{\top}Hx_P\lt\delta$: the projected step stays strictly inside the trust region (the quadratic-model version of their Lemma S.1). (ii) Infeasible $\pi_k$ ($c\gt0$). $\tfrac12x_P^{\top}Hx_P\le\delta+c^2/(2s)=\delta+(b^+)^2\alpha_{\mathrm{KL}}$: exactly the enlarged radius of Theorem 3.2. For the $L_2$ projection no such identity exists; the Euclidean projection is non-expansive in the Euclidean norm, not in the $H$-norm, and can leave the KL trust region even from a feasible policy. In the explorer's default problem the three steps give $g^{\top}x=0.354$ (CPO), $0.324$ (PCPO, KL) and $0.283$ (PCPO, $L_2$). With the KL projection and a feasible iterate, PCPO therefore returns a feasible but generally suboptimal point of CPO's subproblem (the $L_2$ step is feasible in this example too, but not in general), in exchange for never needing a separate recovery rule.
